thread.title: Taiwan Semi: Half In; The Case To Be Long, And When To Be Longer - Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Ltd. (NYSE:TSM)

author: DoctoRx
title: Taiwan Semi: Half In; The Case To Be Long, And When To Be Longer - Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Ltd. (NYSE:TSM)

organizations.name: longer - taiwan semiconductor manufacturing company ltd.

text:
Introduction: reasons to cycle back to TSM There are three reasons I'm writing this article now, before Taiwan Semiconductor ( TSM ) reports Q2 results soon. These are:
it continues my theme of scaling into dips in industry leaders with sensitivity to a good economy there are some interesting points to make about long term projections on a stock I admire this company and think it's relatively undervalued. Beginning with the first point, some top-down thoughts:
Buying the best makes sense now in most sectors I propose a simple double-barreled thesis for readers to consider.
The predicate is that the US is likely in a classic later-cycle expansion where the Fed is restraining growth, with the yield curve is flattening from previous steep (stimulated) levels. Also, sharp increases in both borrowing costs and in fuel prices since their lows of about two years ago should be slowing the economy. I do not expect a recession, but these periods of rising rates A) scare other investors and B) the externalities of higher US rates internationally and the whole trade war stuff can make for challenging economic statistics.
Given all that, the first "barrel" is that it is better to own quality when P/E's face shrinkage as the Fed takes liquidity away. I identify TSM and Intel (NASDAQ: INTC ) as two high quality chip names at low valuations to the S&P 500 ( SPY ). Note that INTC is also a DJIA (NYSEARCA: DIA ) stock and TSM is not part of the SPY, as it is a Taiwanese company. Between TSM and INTC, I prefer TSM for greater consistency of execution and a planned (versus unplanned) management change.
As I discuss later, I think that until the Fed eases, staying with quality in all spaces is optimal from a risk standpoint, and TSM is my favorite choice in the chip sector from a risk-reward standpoint at current prices.
The second "barrel" is my observation that for the last several months, it has been possible to buy industry leaders at similar P/E's as industry laggards, despite point #1 above. Two such examples are Deere ( DE ) versus AGCO ( AGCO ) and Home Depot ( HD ) versus Lowes ( LOW ). Not that there is anything terribly wrong with AGCO and LOW, but their margins and growth records do not compare to the names I mentioned. I made this case recently for JPMorgan Chase ( JPM ) versus, say, BofA ( BAC ). They trade at almost the same forward P/E's, but JPM is a stronger, more diversified franchise with a higher dividend yield.
TSM fits into that theme in a general way, although there are not a lot of pubic foundry competitors to allow a direct comparison.
Thus, top down, I am interested in buying shares of many underappreciated leaders in their fields.
Moving on, TSM has met my expectations....
TSM's future is unfolding as it appeared 4 years ago When I wrote my first TSM article, in April 2014, there was minimal coverage of it in Seeking Alpha . I felt the need in the title to explain that this was actually a very important company, and thus titled it Mega Cap Taiwan Semi Has A Beat And Raise Quarter; Why It's A Core Tech Holding .
Some of what I said then applies today:
The advantages of fabless chip design are so powerful that the foundry business of TSM should have secular growth for many years to come... TSM's advantages of scale and experience, and close relations with industry leaders such as Apple ( AAPL ) give it an advantage that is tough to dislodge. So it may... stay #1 in its industry indefinitely...
Investors may find TSM to be a strong buy and hold investment.
That the same words can be said more than 4 years later is a testament to the solidity of this company, and the semiconductor foundry industry it pioneered.
Also interesting is this interchange with a commenter on my follow-up TSM article three months later, Taiwan Semiconductor Still Dominates; Buying The Sell-Off . That my supposition has held well so far supports the concept that TSM is a superb company, given that AAPL is a perfectionist. First, the comment, then my response (emphasis added):
[Comment] Apple's A8 is a done deal, built at TSMC [i.e., TSM]. The speculations now focus on who will produce Apple’s next processor. There are a lot of related articles and reports on the net. The following is one of such articles. The author claims Apple will stay with TSMC. At this point, I don’t have reliable information to confirm or dispute the claims.
[My response] Re Apple, I would hazard a guess that they are most interested in quality. I would hope that TSMC performs beautifully and that Apple will do its usual thing, which is reward great performance and stay w TSMC. These are two ab-fab companies that are meant for each other .
AAPL now represents about 20% of TSM's revenues if we average 2016 with 2017. TSM keeps making advances in processors and packaging, and AAPL probably implements them first of its clients.
The bigger point here for investors today is that AAPL goes and stays with the best. AAPL is tough, fair, and highly demanding. I think this relationship is strong and a testament to the quality of TSM. So my faith from 4 years ago was rewarded so far.
In the April article, I suggested a valuation metric for TSM:
I argue that a 16X P/E is very attractive and probably a bit low. At $1.50 EPS as my estimate for this year, that suggests a $24 price, which could be appropriate this calendar year.
More to the point, 12% yearly profit growth would lead to a doubling of profits in six years. That would translate to $3.00 EPS in 2020.
Personally, when TSM in fact reached above $23 in November 2014, i.e. to my target price for the year, I sold it to put all my tech dollars back into AAPL. I began trading TSM late last year around $39, but am buying this consolidation more seriously now.
Here we are in mid-2018, and TSM is back on track with the valuation metric I proposed in 2014. At just above $37, it is at 15.9X this year's projected EPS of $2.36 (consensus per ETrade), just about where I thought TSM should trade in the out years. ETrade is showing $2.62 for consensus 2019 EPS, with no estimates shown for 2020. I will project $2.90 EPS for 2020, and project a 15X EPS for mid-2020. That targets $43.50 as a price two years from now, or an 8% CAGR in price over the next two years. Add dividends, and the total return goal is close to 11% per year. However, holding the P/E constant at 16X gives a price target of $46.40, or a CAGR in price of 11.6%; call it 14% per year including dividends.
Given upside to the P/E should TSM begin acting anything like the way it traded in the late '90s and the way many techs trade today, and I like the potential reward here and want to be in this name.
Now for some of the reasons I admire this company so much.
TSM - a superstar company Every field is competitive. Semiconductor development and manufacturing, as a well-known industry of the future, is near the top of that spectrum. Yet, as a start-up in 1987, TSM's capabilities have for some time reached the top of its industry, roughly equal to the larger, and mighty, Samsung ( OTC:SSNLF ). Lately, it appears as though TSM is out-competing the also-mighty Intel ( INTC ). This represents a stellar accomplishment for this company.
TSM has accomplished this while maintaining a fortress balance sheet. It came through the Tech Wreck and Great Recession in good shape. While "Customer A," i.e. AAPL, accounts for about 20% of revenues, its 2017 Business Overview reveals its revenue and product diversity:
465 active customers manufactures more than 9920 different products uses 258 different technologies for its products thus, it is the world’s most diversified and largest provider of logic IC capacity. This is from p. 14 of that document. The points that follow the above ones make what I view as the essence of the case to consider for continued alpha from this name. Strength yields opportunities, as TSM has a single digit percent market share in the approximately $450 B global semiconductor market. Here are some of the points that TSM makes in this report to investors, with emphasis added, and note that this company strives for accuracy rather than hyperbole:
For each new technology node, TSMC has always been the first effective capacity provider in the foundry segment with the best yield and the fastest ramping speed they are using big data to drive further process improvements In 2016 and 2017, they moved in more than 2,300 tools for our 10-nanometer production lines, and once again set a new record in achieving peak output in less than two months .
No wonder TSM is gaining share in the foundry industry. The company has projected a 4% CAGR for the industry as a whole through 2022, but expects the foundry business - where it increased its share to 56% last year - to grow much faster than that. There are no guarantees, but the immense cost of next-gen products and the know-how required to manufacture them with high yields makes me satisfied that TSM is well-positioned to grow its market share within its industry.
In addition, while there are reams that any of us could point to about this company, another point I liked in the more detailed Annual Report includes TSM improving on old nodes to provide useful technologies in several ways (see pp. 76-77). While we focus on pushing the envelope for growth, there good profit potential remains from prior nodes as they acquire new capabilities that meet the needs of the marketplace.
I think that TSM's top-tier qualities argue for a premium valuation, not a mildly sub-market one. Interested investors may wish to look at this stock for this core reason.
Risks: Part 1 The semiconductor industry is notoriously cyclical. People get excited about how chip-driven products will change the world. Capital enters the tech industry, then it floods in. At some point, the future does not meet expectations, and the whole tech ecosystem retrenches. Perhaps this process has again begun.
TSM lowered guidance in April, pointing to weaker smartphone markets than it expected when it guided in January. It is also cautious on the crypto business, which drives sales of high-performing, expensive chips. (Robert Castellano has an informative article on this topic that is not behind a firewall.)
Beyond the usual market risks, there are always company-specific risks. The founder, longtime CEO and until June the only chairman that TSM has known, "Morris" Chang, has retired. New chairman Mark Liu and CEO C.C. Wei are veterans at TSM, but the absence of Dr. Chang imparts extra risk. Many other risks apply. One key risk is that as TSM moves to greater complexity of its most cutting-edge chips, i.e. 5 nm and lower nodes, it is implementing ASML's ( ASML ) EUV solutions. While TSM and ASML are both expressing confidence that enough of the practical problems have been solved to make the 5 and 3 nm nodes financially successful for TSM, there are no certainties here. (TSM is an investor in ASML along with INTC and SSNLF.)
Two other matters to be considered are, first, politics - the issue of Taiwan as the Republic of China rather than a province of the PRC may not end well for TSM's shareholders. And, the geology of the region, which is susceptible to earthquakes, provides another risk.
A different big-picture risk is discussed next.
Risks: long term technology considerations I think about what comes next for the chip industry, even assuming that EUV presents years of opportunity. Semicon Taiwan has a PowerPoint up that discusses what comes next after FinFETs. Much of it is accessible in the general case to investors and other interested parties who are not professionals in the field of transistors. For example, you may find Slide 6 very relevant. It shows a potential technology road map beyond FinFETs. This gets discussed in some detail beginning with Slide 26, where next-gen technologies such as tunnel FETs (3D and 2D), negative capacitance FETs and spin wave devices are discussed.
My takeaway is that of an investor who was interested enough in tech to attend a 2-month university-level computing/semiconductor curriculum in the summer of '67 while in high school. The "-tronics" craze was peaking on Wall Street around then. I have seen many cycles since then. The following years were dismal for most stocks, including tech stocks. Texas Instruments, for example, went absolutely nowhere from 1972 to 1991. IBM peaked in 1968 at around $18.50 (split-adjusted), a price it was still at in 1982. That was bad enough; it bottomed around $10 in 1993. (Data from Yahoo Finance charts.) For people who thought Warren Buffett was just a fuddy-duddy for not joining the tech craze in the '90s, these and many other examples (including much worse stocks) show why. Tech trends are tough to predict beyond a certain time frame.
I expect and am willing to put money at risk that if there is enough utility from new products, there will be technical solutions found to keep the whole computing process moving forward well into the 2030s. Whether Moore's Law will hold precisely is of some relevance, but not key. I think that TSM investors may wish to wonder whether, and when, its field will become mature, leaving TSM to be a consolidator in that maturing field. Or, will semiconductors or whatever follows them to speed computing up further, make it more efficient, etc., will remain an exciting true secular growth field. I am bullish, though, on the commercial prospects of better tech-infused products across the entire global economy.
In summary, a risk I think about is that even if EUV pans out and drives superior microprocessors through the 2020-30 time frame, with growing profits for TSM, if that technology allows cost-effective production of all that society really needs out of computing units, the question of what an attractive P/E for TSM really is needs to be rethought.
I temper this risk with the thought that EUV has promise for years to come, and as a B2B tech intermediary, TSM can be agnostic as to which technologies are going to make the grade in the future, and that something will be there when needed.
Some considerations of TSM as an ADR Some comments on the situation I believe to be the case; please verify this for your own situation if interested in TSM ADRs.
TSM trades in the US as an ADR. Citi handles these .
The conversion ratio is 5 ordinary shares per one ADR.
It appears that the withholding rate on the once-yearly dividends, which went ex last month, is 21% for US investors. Residents of other countries may have lower rates .
Because TSM has been paying dividends only once a year, I believe that they are as good for trading in an IRA as a stock whose dividends are "qualified" under IRS rules. The withholding normally can come back only in a taxable account, though.
TSM cheap enough for a half-stake; why only half The main thesis I have is that TSM is again at a sound fundamental entry point for long term investors. It may be simplistic, but I posit that past can be assumed to be prologue, per the long term performance of TSM versus the SPY. TSM is up 10X over the past 20 years, whereas the SPY is up 2X. That's a 5X outperformance.
In addition to following the long term trend here, TSM could be a beneficiary of the trade conflict between the US and China.
My caution on TSM begins with the guidance, the never-one-roach theory of investing. I did buy in last week at $36.43 and plan to keep, not trade, the shares (unless they soar for no reason). The purchase is on the basis that a 20% off sale on TSM can be bought outside of a recession.
The hesitancy to go to a full position on this name also relates to a 5-year chart of TSM, the tech sector ( QQQ ) and the SPY:
TSM data by YCharts
Everything is up a lot, which is one reason for general caution. A second reason for caution is that tech is up a lot more than the general market; note that the SPY ex-tech would be up much less than the 60% shown. Yet my observation over 50+ years of following markets is that reversion to the mean is a powerful force, and that periods where the Fed makes money scarcer tend to be catalytic periods for that process to occur. The tech trends are mixed. Unit sales of many electronic devices, small ones such as smartphones to large ones such as TVs, are flat to down. Crypto is unpredictable. AI and self-driving cars, two of the next new things, are not big markets yet; the timing and extent of them really moving the needle for the semiconductor industry is also unpredictable.
So we could once again be at a resting period for TSM's end markets between two waves of the tech sea, in which case a 16X P/E will probably appear too high.
Finally, there is the strangely-repeating tendency of hot, or hot-turned-cooling, sectors to cool off in the July-October period.
Having cut back a lot on tech in late January, I am edging back into the sector where I see long term value, which I see in TSM. But I'm not all "there" yet for the sector on a shorter-term basis. Thus, a half-stake to where I would ordinarily want to be in this name, given my view that the world is not close to the later innings of a digitally-driven transformation.
Conclusions - TSM as a superior B2B play To summarize, TSM is an innovator and highly competent technology implementer. It created the independent foundry business and dominates it to this day. It enjoys economies of scale and numerous core and non-core competencies that may allow it to gain market share in a growing semiconductor industry for years to come. The company has basically met the expectations I laid out for it 4 years ago, which reinforces my confidence in its ongoing capabilities, and is paying healthy dividends while maintaining a powerful balance sheet.
Despite this, TSM trades at or below the multiple of the SPY.
TSM thus fits into a theme I have been reporting on this year, in which leading companies in important sectors of the economy are often trading relatively cheap to the market. It was nice to see this weekend's Barron's highlight not just one such stock, but two I have mentioned recently, namely Toll Brothers ( TOL ) and Royal Caribbean ( RCL ). I have several chips down on these sorts of relative value stocks, and TSM is now (once again) one of them.
Among the many risks to TSM are downside cyclicality of the industry, the management change, and a fallow stretch for tech sales to end users.
I propose that a reasonable first downside target for bargain-hunters is suggested both fundamentally and by the chart to be $35. There is stronger chart support around $30, going back to 2016 into 2017. Lower prices than $30 might be seen in a recession or if the EUV technology does not allow TSM to migrate to the 5 nm and then 3 nm node with acceptable results. I would be prepared to scale in deeper to TSM at or below $35 if the general story remains unchanged. We will learn more when Q2 results are released before the US markets open on July 19.
Submitted Sunday with TSM at $37.27 at Friday's close.
Thanks for reading and sharing any comments you wish to contribute.
Disclosure: I am/we are long TSM,AAPL,DE,HD,JPM, RCL,TOL.
I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions. I am not receiving compensation for it (other than from Seeking Alpha). I have no business relationship with any company whose stock is mentioned in this article.
